title: Think Strategy Is Just Logic? Think Again
author: Colette Molteni
summary: Molteni argues that strategy cannot be treated as pure logic, because the people who must act on it respond to feeling, timing and trust as much as to data. Drawing on Goleman-style emotional intelligence and her own decade in tech data analytics, she shows how leaders mistake polite nods for buy-in. She uses a personal story of being pitched an investment while broke to illustrate that even sound strategy fails when timing and empathy are ignored. She then contrasts a 44-slide kickoff deck with the rapport-building conversation she would have run instead. The move throughout is to reposition emotional intelligence, meaning empathy, social awareness and relationship management, as a core input to execution rather than a soft add-on. It sits in Leadership because it is about persuading, reading a room and driving change among adults at work.
points: Logic alone does not produce buy-in; leaders must read the mood of the room, because nods can signal politeness or pressure rather than agreement.
Timing and framing are strategic levers: a well-reasoned plan delivered when a team is burned out or territorial can die on arrival.
Trust is built through listening and rapport before facts, illustrated by a 44-slide kickoff deck that earned no trust from a technical audience.
Numbers must be contextualized against the intangible, since irrational feelings can still break a highly logical strategy.
The author recasts emotional intelligence (empathy, social awareness, relationship management) as the working inputs that turn a strategy document into a plan people act on.
quotes: People, whether direct reports or leaders, cannot be convinced to move a certain way based on logic alone. If logic alone worked, think of all the times someone does something they should not do despite knowing better?
The point is that you cannot just appeal to the logic of the people you are trying to get buy-in from. Nods can be a sign of simple politeness or pressure from being observed, not actual agreement.

Even the most logical strategic decision can backfire if it's delivered at the wrong moment or in the wrong way. Social awareness means tuning into your team and organization's mood, culture, and unspoken dynamics.
If you can't get around the timing, think how you can still be an empathy catalyst. What will appeal to their needs and wants? What do they get out of the strategy?

If you want your strategy to do more than gather digital dust, treat emotional intelligence as a core input—not an afterthought. Empathy helps you see around corners. Social awareness enables you to steer with context.
The feelings can be overpowering and even illogical. But no matter how irrational, they can still break the highly logical strategy you are attempting to implement.
